title: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE BIBLE VERSE THAT COULD BE DESTROYING YOUR SOUL IF YOU READ IT WRONG
paragraphs: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE BIBLE VERSE THAT COULD BE DESTROYING YOUR SOUL IF YOU READ IT WRONG
Paul never gave Christians permission to live however they wanted. He exposed a dangerous kind of freedom—one that can leave you smiling in public while quietly becoming a prisoner in private.
There is a frightening possibility that deserves your attention.
You can be doing something that isn't explicitly forbidden in Scripture… and still be allowing it to slowly destroy the person God is calling you to become.
Read that again.
Because some of the most dangerous things in your spiritual life don't arrive looking like sin.
They arrive looking like freedom.

A harmless conversation. An innocent attraction. Another hour scrolling. A private habit nobody knows about. A relationship you keep defending. A form of entertainment that gradually makes darkness feel normal.
And somewhere in the middle of it all, you whisper the words that have become the favorite defense of countless Christians:
“But I'm free in Christ.”
Yes. You are.
But free to do what?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if the thing you keep defending as your freedom is the very thing that has begun to master you?
Nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul confronted this dangerous confusion in a church that looked surprisingly familiar.
The believers in Corinth lived in a wealthy, influential, morally complicated city. They were surrounded by competing philosophies, religious practices, social pressures, and sexual immorality.
And the church was struggling.

They possessed spiritual gifts, but they were divided. They celebrated knowledge, but sometimes lacked love. They understood that Christ had brought freedom, yet some were apparently using that freedom to justify behavior that contradicted their new identity in Him.
Then Paul wrote words that would confront generations of believers:
“Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.
— 1 Corinthians 6:12, translated from the Greek
Those words sound simple.
Until you realize Paul was not merely asking whether Christians were allowed to do something.
He was asking whether that something was beginning to own them.
And the difference could change your entire life.
In the original Greek, the statement translated “Everything is permissible for me” reads:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν — Panta moi exestin.
Literally, “All things are lawful for me,” or “All things are permitted to me.”
But here is a detail many readers miss.

Paul repeats the phrase and immediately qualifies it. Many biblical scholars understand “All things are lawful for me” as a slogan circulating among the Corinthians, which Paul quotes in order to challenge its misuse.

The Greek manuscripts do not contain our modern quotation marks, so interpreters must recognize the possible slogan from the context. Either way, Paul's argument is unmistakable: Christian freedom cannot be separated from what is beneficial, what builds up others, and what honors the Lord.
Paul continues:
ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει — all’ ou panta sympherei.
“But not all things are beneficial.”
The verb sympherei carries the sense of being advantageous, profitable, or helpful.
Paul was challenging believers to think beyond the question of permission.
Something may be permitted without being spiritually helpful.
Something may be enjoyable without being wise.
Something may be socially acceptable without being worthy of your devotion.
And something may begin as a choice but eventually become a chain.
Then comes Paul's devastating declaration:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος — all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
“But I will not be mastered by anything.”
Notice the relationship between the words.
The Greek verb exestin concerns what is permitted or authorized. The verb exousiasthēsomai concerns being brought under someone's or something's authority.
Paul is making a striking contrast.
You may claim authority to choose something.
But what happens when that thing begins exercising authority over you?
You say you can stop whenever you want.
But can you?
You say the relationship isn't affecting your walk with God.
But why are you hiding parts of it?
You say the entertainment is harmless.
But why does your heart feel increasingly comfortable with what once troubled your conscience?
You say you are simply enjoying your freedom.
But why does surrendering that pleasure feel almost unbearable?
This is where Paul's words stop being a theological discussion and become a mirror.
Because there is a difference between having access to something and having freedom from it.
And sometimes the clearest evidence that something has gained too much power over your heart is how fiercely you defend your right to keep it.
Think about that.
You might not be addicted to a substance.
You might be addicted to approval.
You might not be trapped in an obviously destructive relationship.
You might be trapped in the fear of being alone.
You might not be worshiping a carved idol.
You might be giving your identity, peace, and emotional stability to money, recognition, success, attention, or the opinion of someone who barely thinks about you.
Not every strong desire is an addiction. Not every enjoyment is idolatry. Scripture does not condemn every ordinary pleasure.
But even good things can become disordered when they occupy a place in our hearts that belongs to God.
And Paul is asking us to examine that possibility.
Not so we can become terrified of every decision.
But so we can stop confusing freedom with the absence of restraint.
Because biblical freedom is something far more beautiful than simply getting to do whatever we want.
It is the freedom to belong to Jesus without being enslaved by lesser masters.
And that brings us to the part of the passage that changes everything.
Paul does not leave his argument hanging in the air.
He brings it directly to the human body, sexual immorality, and our union with Christ.
In 1 Corinthians 6:13–20, Paul reminds believers that the body is not meant for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
He points to the resurrection of Jesus.
He reminds Christians that their bodies are members of Christ.
And then he makes an astonishing declaration:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV
Stop there.
You are not your own.
In a world constantly telling you that ultimate freedom means belonging to nobody but yourself, Scripture announces something radically different.
You belong to the One who loved you enough to redeem you.
Not because God sees you as an object to control.
Not because Jesus came to steal your joy.
But because sin had already shown what cruel mastery looks like.
And Christ came to rescue you.
The price Paul speaks of points to the saving work of Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners.
Your body matters because Christ has redeemed you.
Your choices matter because your life belongs to Him.
Your freedom matters because it was purchased through His sacrifice.
Christian obedience, then, is not an attempt to purchase God's love.
It is a response to the love that has already been revealed in Jesus.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come to make sin more convenient.
He came to save sinners.
He did not shed His blood so we could rename bondage as freedom.
He gave Himself to bring us out of bondage and into a new life.
And He did not rise from the dead merely to improve our public image.
He rose so that those who belong to Him might walk in newness of life.
But perhaps you are reading this while carrying something you have never told another person.
A struggle that keeps returning.
A temptation you promised God you would resist.
A secret that makes you feel like two different people.
The believer everyone sees.
And the exhausted person you meet when the door closes.
You love Jesus.
You know what Scripture says.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have made promises.
And somehow, you keep finding yourself back in the same place.
Afterward comes the silence.
The shame.
The familiar thought:
“Maybe I'm not really changing.”
Perhaps you've even begun avoiding prayer because you cannot bear to approach God with another confession.
Listen carefully.
The fact that you need repentance does not mean you are beyond redemption.
But neither does God's mercy mean your sin is harmless.
Both truths matter.
Jesus does not call us to pretend that darkness is light.
And He does not tell repentant sinners that darkness has the final word.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
The religious leaders placed her in the middle of a public confrontation over adultery. Her wrongdoing had become the center of a spectacle.
Jesus refused to participate in their self-righteous cruelty.
After her accusers departed, He said:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
— John 8:11, ESV
Do you see it?
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Jesus did not say adultery was acceptable.
He did not say her past defined her forever.
He did not excuse her sin, and He did not join her accusers in using her humiliation as entertainment.
He called her toward a different future.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes a new beginning possible.
And this is why Paul's words about freedom are not an attack on joy.
They are a rescue mission.
Because sin has a way of making promises it cannot keep.
It promises relief and leaves you restless.
It promises intimacy and sometimes leaves you more isolated.
It promises control and gradually demands more.
It promises freedom while quietly building a prison around your desires.
Not every struggle follows the same pattern, and not every painful consequence can be traced to personal sin. But when a desire begins to rule us, Paul's warning becomes painfully relevant.
“I will not be mastered by anything.”
Those words should make us examine the things we have stopped questioning.
And perhaps the question is not merely whether you are allowed to watch it, buy it, pursue it, post it, or participate in it.
Perhaps the question is what it is doing to your heart.
Is it helping you love God more faithfully?
Is it strengthening or weakening your self-control?
Is it shaping you toward truth or making deception easier?
Is it building up the people around you?
Can you receive it with gratitude and walk away from it freely?
Or has it begun demanding a place in your life that you are unwilling to surrender?
Paul returns to the same principle in 1 Corinthians 10:23:
“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up.
— ESV
Then, in the following verse, he turns our attention toward others:
“Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.”
— 1 Corinthians 10:24, ESV
Now the picture becomes even clearer.
Christian freedom is not only about what a choice does to you.
It is also about what your choices do to others.
In the immediate context of 1 Corinthians 10, Paul is discussing food associated with idols, matters of conscience, and the importance of not causing unnecessary harm to others.
He is not teaching that every personal preference must become a universal law.
He is teaching believers to exercise their freedom with wisdom and love.
That distinction matters.
Some Christians have used passages like this to impose human rules where Scripture has not established them.
They have treated personal convictions as though they were commandments from God.
They have made other believers feel guilty for enjoying legitimate gifts.
But Paul was not replacing freedom in Christ with a new system of man-made bondage.
Romans 14 reminds us that believers must not despise or condemn one another over genuinely disputable matters.
At the same time, freedom must never become an excuse for what Scripture clearly identifies as sin.
Paul makes that plain in Galatians 5:13:
“For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.”
— ESV
There it is.
Freedom that serves.
Freedom that loves.
Freedom that refuses to make self-indulgence the center of everything.
Freedom that is strong enough to say no.
And sometimes, saying no is not the loss of freedom.
It is the evidence that freedom is beginning to grow.
Imagine someone who once could not go a day without returning to a destructive habit.
Then, through prayer, repentance, honest accountability, wise support, and the transforming work of God, that person begins to experience change.
The struggle may not disappear overnight.
There may be setbacks.
There may be tears.
There may be difficult conversations and decisions that cost something.
But little by little, the old master loses its unquestioned authority.
That is not merely behavior modification.
For the Christian, genuine transformation is rooted in a deeper reality: belonging to Jesus Christ and learning to walk by His Spirit.
Romans 6:14 declares:
“For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.”
— ESV
Paul is not promising that Christians will never experience temptation again.
Nor is he suggesting that believers can reach a state where they no longer need confession, humility, or dependence on God.
He is announcing that sin is no longer the rightful ruler of those who belong to Christ.
The power of sin has been decisively challenged through the death and resurrection of Jesus.
And that truth changes how we fight.
We do not fight for God's acceptance as though Christ has done nothing.
We fight from the grace we have received.
We do not repent to convince Jesus to begin loving us.
We repent because His mercy calls us out of what destroys us.
We do not pursue holiness to make ourselves superior to other people.
We pursue holiness because the Savior who rescued us is holy.
And sometimes the first step toward freedom is the confession we have been avoiding.
“Lord, this has more power over me than I wanted to admit.”
“Lord, I have been defending what I should have surrendered.”
“Lord, I have confused Your patience with Your approval.”
“Lord, I want You more than I want this sin, but I need Your help.”
There is no need to make those words impressive.
God is not waiting for a beautifully written speech.
He calls us to come truthfully.
First John 1:9 gives believers this assurance:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— ESV
Notice where the confidence rests.
Not in the perfection of our confession.
Not in the intensity of our emotions.
Not in how long we have managed to avoid failure.
Our confidence rests in God's faithfulness and justice, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
That is why shame does not have to write the final chapter.
Your past may be real.
Your consequences may be real.
The people you hurt may need time, restitution, and evidence of genuine change.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
But your failures do not possess greater saving power than the crucified and risen Christ.
The cross is not permission to remain in chains. It is the announcement that the chains do not have to remain your master.
And if you have been struggling in secret, perhaps today is the day to stop fighting entirely alone.
Talk to a mature, trustworthy Christian.
Seek pastoral care.
Where addiction, trauma, or serious emotional distress is involved, seek qualified professional support as well.
There is no shame in receiving appropriate help.
God often works through the care, wisdom, prayers, and faithful presence of other people.
You do not have to announce every private struggle to the world.
But you also do not have to build your life around hiding.
James 5:16 calls believers to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another.
That is not an invitation to public humiliation.
It is an invitation into the healing honesty of Christian community.
And perhaps this is where Paul's teaching becomes most personal.
Because the real question is not simply, “Can I do this?”
The deeper question is:
“Does this choice reflect the life Jesus gave Himself to redeem?”
There are decisions where Scripture speaks directly, and obedience is required.
There are other decisions where we must apply biblical wisdom, examine our motives, consider our conscience, and think about the good of others.
Not everything permissible is beneficial.
Not everything beneficial in one circumstance is wise in another.
And not everything we desire deserves authority over our lives.
This is not about becoming a person who never laughs, celebrates, enjoys good food, appreciates beauty, or experiences the legitimate pleasures of God's creation.
The Bible teaches us to receive God's gifts with thanksgiving.
It is about refusing to turn those gifts into gods.
It is about enjoying what is good without becoming enslaved to it.
It is about learning that the greatest treasure of the Christian life is not unlimited access to every earthly experience.
It is Jesus Christ Himself.
And when He becomes our greatest treasure, even our understanding of freedom begins to change.
We start asking different questions.
Not merely, “How close can I get to sin without crossing the line?”
But, “How faithfully can I walk with the One who saved me?”
Not merely, “What am I allowed to keep?”
But, “What is keeping me from wholehearted obedience?”
Not merely, “Will anyone find out?”
But, “Am I living truthfully before the God who already knows me and still calls me to Himself?”
This is the freedom Paul wanted the Corinthians to understand.
And it is the freedom our generation desperately needs.
A generation surrounded by choices can still be deeply enslaved.
A person with thousands of followers can still be desperate for approval.
Someone with financial success can still be ruled by greed.
A person who can access nearly any form of entertainment can still be unable to sit quietly with their own thoughts.
And a Christian who knows all the language of grace can still be resisting the very transformation that grace teaches us to pursue.
Titus 2:11–12 tells us that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.
Grace does not merely forgive.
Grace also teaches.
Grace restores.
Grace reshapes our desires.
And grace continually points us back to the Savior who makes new life possible.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior has never been about pretending that believers have spotless histories.
It is about proclaiming that Jesus Christ is able to redeem people whose histories are anything but spotless.
From hiding to confession.
From rebellion to repentance.
From self-righteousness to humility.
From bondage to the freedom found in Christ.
Not because we are powerful enough to rewrite ourselves.
But because Jesus is the Savior who redeems sinners and transforms lives.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, please do not rush past that moment.
If you are still fighting a battle that others cannot see, you can simply comment, “I'm still fighting.”

And if God has already brought you through a season of bondage, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness. Someone reading the comments may need to know that repentance, healing, and restoration are possible.
Your testimony does not have to be dramatic to glorify Jesus.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
“I used to defend what was destroying me. By God's grace, I am learning to surrender it.”
And maybe someone you love needs to hear this message too.
A son or daughter struggling with temptation.
A friend who has mistaken God's patience for permission.
A believer who has been quietly losing hope.
Or someone who has never understood why the Gospel offers more than a list of religious rules.
You may never know who reads it silently.
You may never know whose conscience is awakened, whose prayer begins, or whose understanding of grace changes because they encountered the truth of Scripture.
But every sincere opportunity to point someone toward Jesus matters.
Come back to 1 Corinthians 6:12 when a decision feels complicated.
Read it again when a habit begins demanding more than it should.
Remember it when you are tempted to ask only whether something is allowed.
Then keep reading through verse 20.
Because the answer to a life of holy freedom is not merely stronger willpower.
It is remembering whose you are.
And if you believe this message deserves to reach beyond your own screen, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing Scripture-centered teaching, Christian encouragement, discipleship resources, and the message of redemption through Jesus Christ.
Those free resources are part of a larger desire: to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in discernment, develop spiritual maturity, and remain rooted in Christ.
But meaningful ministry requires real work.
Writing, research, resource preparation, outreach, and the continued development of discipleship materials all require time and support.
And this is where your partnership can make a difference.
It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand the work so that more people can encounter the Gospel, study the Scriptures, and receive Christian encouragement.

Scripture encourages believers to support faithful Gospel work, as seen in Galatians 6:6 and 1 Corinthians 9:14. It also teaches that giving should be willing rather than pressured, as 2 Corinthians 9:7 makes clear.
You can glorify Him through faithful obedience, prayer, service, generosity, sharing the Gospel, and countless acts of love.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the continuation of Gospel-centered resources.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
The free resources remain an invitation to grow, and your prayers, encouragement, comments, shares, and willingness to invite others into biblical discipleship also matter.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still asking questions about Christianity to follow along.
Because the goal is not to build a crowd that admires a page.
It is to point people toward a Savior worthy of their lives.
And before you leave, I want you to return to the question that began this entire conversation.
What if something you call freedom is actually mastering you?
Don't answer too quickly.
Bring it before the Lord.
Let His Word examine your motives.
Ask Him for wisdom where Scripture leaves room for discernment and courage where Scripture calls for obedience.
And if you discover that something has gained a hold on your heart, do not surrender to despair.
Surrender to Christ.
The Savior who died for sinners is not powerless before your struggle.
The One who rose from the grave is not defeated by your past.
And the Lord who calls you to holiness is also the Lord who supplies grace for the journey.
You may have spent years asking, “Am I allowed to do this?”
Perhaps today, for the first time, you are ready to ask something greater.
“Jesus, does this help me love You, obey You, and become more like You?”
That question may cost you something.
A habit.
A relationship that continually draws you into sin.
An unhealthy source of validation.
A secret compromise.
A version of yourself you have spent years protecting.
But whatever repentance requires you to leave behind, Christ Himself is worth more.
And when the struggle feels overwhelming, remember that Christian freedom does not begin with your ability to save yourself.
It begins with the Savior who has already accomplished what you never could.
So come to Him.
Not tomorrow, when you think you will be stronger.
Not someday, when your life looks more respectable.
Come with the truth.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come trusting the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest tragedy is not that you once lived in chains.
It is to hear the Gospel of freedom and insist that your chains are all you ever wanted.
You were not redeemed by the blood of Jesus merely to defend the prison He came to bring you out of.
